prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints tie credit to asset prices, so that shocks are amplified and propagated through the economy

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) isolate a single, transparent mechanism: borrowing limits depend on collateral values, and collateral values depend on the borrowing that the limits permit. That feedback turns small, temporary shocks into large and persistent fluctuations. The mechanism is general and tractable, and it became the foundation for later financial-friction models in macro-finance. It is almost thirty years old, so the debate over its validity has had time to settle. Attribution is also unusually clean, because the 1997 paper is a two-author origin point. As a mechanism designer, I value a contribution that states its assumptions precisely and yields a result others could build on. Opening rankings are not evidence of merit, but they do show that members from several fields reached this candidate by different routes.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap. The 2022 prize recognised banks and financial crises, and the committee may judge that the financial-frictions territory is already covered. The mechanism is also primarily theoretical, and direct empirical identification of the collateral channel is harder than the theory suggests. A two-name award leaves out the financial-accelerator strand (Gertler, Gilchrist), which has a stronger quantitative and empirical side and arguably more direct policy influence. A committee that values empirical confirmation and breadth of use could reasonably prefer the heterogeneous-firm trade candidate (B005), which has wider support across the opening rankings.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B011 first but proposes adding Gertler as a third name, treating Gertler's financial-accelerator work as part of the intellectual core while noting that the overlap with Bernanke's 2022 prize makes this addition delicate.
responses.response: I take the point that Gertler's contribution to quantitative macro models used in policy is substantial. My view is that it is a distinct strand and should not be bundled into the prize for the collateral-price feedback. The accelerator lineage is the part most entangled with the 2022 recognition, so adding Gertler raises the very overlap question that weighs against B011. Gertler also appears in the New Keynesian entry (B019), so crediting him here would blur two achievements. I keep the award to Kiyotaki and Moore, and I would revisit this only if the committee concludes that the accelerator strand is not covered by the 2022 prize.

responses.point: Friberg ranks heterogeneous-firm trade (B005) first. He sees it as a foundational and general framework, confirmed across many datasets, that underpins large empirical and policy literatures, and he treats the overlap with Krugman's 2008 prize as only partial.
responses.response: I agree that B005 is a strong candidate. It was my own third choice, and its breadth of empirical confirmation is a real advantage over B011, whose empirical identification is more indirect. I still rank B011 higher because its attribution is cleaner. Melitz (2003) is the central model, but the Helpman credit depends on a broader programme that Krugman's prize partly covers. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are also outside the credited names, as several colleagues note. I do not see this as a decisive difference in scientific merit, and I list B005 as my first alternative. If the committee settles the attribution question for B005 convincingly, I could support it.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks the New Keynesian framework (B019) first. He ranks B011 sixth, citing overlap with the 2022 prize, split credit because Gertler appears in two entries, and the difficulty of identifying the amplification mechanism empirically.
responses.response: The overlap and identification concerns are the most serious objections to B011, and I list them among my own uncertainties. I would answer in two parts. First, the 2022 prize concerned the role of banks and bank runs in crises, whereas Kiyotaki–Moore concerns collateral and asset-price feedback in the real economy. These are related, but I do not read the second as a subset of the first. Second, B019 has the opposite problem. It is mature and influential, but by your own account and others' it credits eight people, and any three-person selection omits major contributors. For a prize that has to name specific people for a specific discovery, I weigh the clean two-name attribution of B011 more heavily than I weigh the practical reach of B019.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson also ranks B011 first and proposes Gertler as a third name. She argues that his independent contributions to credit frictions in monetary policy models survive the overlap with Bernanke's 2022 recognition, and she leaves Gilchrist out only to respect the three-name limit.
responses.response: I agree that Gertler's independent contributions are real. The question is whether they belong to this discovery. If the committee wants an award on credit frictions broadly, then Gertler and possibly Gilchrist are legitimate. That is a different citation from the one I propose, and it would need to be argued on its own terms. For this proposal I prefer the narrower citation, which can be defended on the originating mechanism alone. I would not oppose a three-name version if a majority prefers it, but I think it weakens the attribution argument.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises as having already covered collateral-based amplification, which would lower the marginal case for B011.
Whether Gertler (and Gilchrist) should be credited for the financial-accelerator strand, either within B011 or as part of a separate achievement.
How much weight the committee places on indirect empirical identification of the collateral channel compared with the more directly confirmed trade candidate B005.

My own B048 ranking (alternating-offers bargaining) rests on strong timing and attribution arguments, but opening support for it was thin. I am not proposing it as the main configuration, and I have not tried to pair it with B011 because of the three-person limit. These assessments rest on general knowledge and have not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile: it lists no co-authorship, institutional or other connection to Kiyotaki, Moore, or the other credited names in B011, B005 or B048. B048 is adjacent to my microeconomic-theory and market-design background, but the profile identifies no personal connection to its candidates.
